Recognizing defaults as choices made for us by someone else is the first step towards changing our relationship with defaults.
Beginning a class with a conversation or with some quiet writing in journals or with group work at the board are all device-free, AI-resistant learning strategies.
We should not treat the decision to allow or restrict technology as equivalent to teaching students how to use it.
Treating AI as just another tool to add to our classroom toolkit misses how fundamentally AI is changing the nature of knowledge, learning, and even what it means to be educated.

t: Fading Support
q: Fading is the missing half of scaffolding — it is not a separate idea, but the part of the sequence that turns temporary support into independent capability.
Removing the end of the worked solution first produced the strongest results. This is the opposite of what most teachers do instinctively.
Fading is associated with fewer unproductive learning events and, thereby, lends itself to better learning outcomes." — Alexander Renkl, Robert Atkinson and Cornelia Große (2004)
These 'ignored impasses' were linked to poorer performance on both similar and new problems.

t: Burning the Lifeboat for Warmth
q: The underlying condition is that the university has been selling a bundle that was only ever bundled because the components were technologically inseparable.
Information is no longer scarce. It has been getting less scarce since Gutenberg, then the internet made it free, and now AI makes it not just free but responsive.
AI doesn't just erode the teaching pillar. It simultaneously detonates the credentialing pillar.
The signal and the substance both got hit by the same weapon at the same time.
The ones that refuse to ask it are burning the lifeboat for warmth.

t: Attention by Design: Why I Refuse to Gild My Teaching and My Classroom
q: Before new information can enter working memory and be encoded into long-term memory, students must first attend to it.
Every visual display competes, to some degree, for students' limited attention.
Dozens of displays collectively increase the amount of information in the environment students must continually attempt to ignore.
These environmental decisions are grounded in what I know about attention and working memory and not my own personality and hobbies.
Students experience a welcoming classroom through effective praise, positive relationships, consistent routines, and a teacher who is genuinely invested in them.

t: Argumentation Belongs in Every Classroom
q: Instructional redesign should come before AI integration. Schools keep acquiring the technology first and asking what to do with it second.

Nothing teaches argumentation like a fight nobody has settled yet — the textbook controversy has an answer waiting in the back of the book, but a live one forces students to do what adults are doing right now.
The warrant is the part almost everyone skips, and it is where arguments are actually won and lost.
Say the warrant out loud and suddenly there is something to debate.
The argumentation structure is the constant; the controversy is a plug-in.

t: "Am I Just a Loser?"
q: I know this sounds dramatic, but... what is wrong with me? Am I unable to get the jobs I want? Am I just a total loser?
Eleven final-round interviews is enough data that I don't think this is random anymore. I think something is going on.
The good news is that if there's a pattern, there's probably an addressable cause.
What he is experiencing is not a character flaw or a permanent condition. Rather it is a behavior to identify and improve.
Ram was highly competent but was presenting himself with insufficient confidence and executive presence in final-round interviews, which decision-makers read as uncertainty.

t: i-Ready Finally Has Real Research…And It Changes Nothing
q: That has finally changed. Last month, Online Learning – a Q1 educational journal – published the strongest evaluation of i-Ready to date.

'Our analyses are descriptive versus causal, as we cannot fully…understand or account for selection into treatment…[and] we were unable to account for other recovery interventions occurring during the same period.' That sentence gives me confidence in the paper: rather than overselling the findings, the authors openly acknowledge exactly what their design can (and cannot) tell us.
After two years, students who used i-Ready scored approximately: +0.04 standard deviations higher in Reading, +0.04 standard deviations higher in Math. That's it. That's the headline.
Ironically, the research so many people have been waiting for ultimately changes nothing: the evidence is stronger, but the conclusion remains the same.
The 'weeks of learning' reported in this paper is an inference, not an observed result. Accordingly, although it may make for an appealing headline, it is much less scientifically convincing.
Extrapolated, that suggests between $500,000 and $1 million dollars were spent for each 0.01 standard deviation growth amongst users: a substantially altered cost-benefit calculation.

t: Your syllabus needs an enemy
q: Every document in my course was approved by a committee of one. I wrote the syllabus, I revised the syllabus, I approved the syllabus. Same committee every time. It has never once sent my work back.

Students are not that committee. They read the syllabus like opposing counsel: hunting the late-policy loophole, the contradiction between page 2 and the LMS, the assignment description vague enough to argue about in week 12.

'You are three readers reviewing my syllabus, and none of you are being polite. Reader 1 is a grade-focused student hunting for loopholes, contradictions, and anything vague enough to dispute later. Reader 2 is a skeptical senior colleague who thinks my policies are either toothless or theatrical, and says which. Reader 3 is an overwhelmed first-generation student who flags every place the document assumes knowledge nobody gave them.'

It takes ten minutes. You'll fix two things before fall that would cost you a bunch of email threads in October, and the first-gen reader will catch something that's been invisible to you for years, because you wrote the document for a student you stopped being decades ago.
The reflex is the point: nothing student-facing ships without a hostile read first.
Borrow a trick from every other craft: get a hostile read before the real audience arrives.

t: The Problem with Transferable Skills
q: Despite the current vogue for attempting to teach transferable skills rather than specific knowledge, the best evidence we have indicates that it is not possible.
improvement in any single mental function rarely brings about equal improvement in any other function.

Our cognition is tightly bound to specific contexts. Hard work and good teaching may allow us to transfer our skills to closely related domains—so-called near transfer—but far transfer of skills is elusive.

if you remind a student to 'look at an issue from multiple perspectives' often enough, he will learn that he ought to do so, but if he doesn't know much about an issue, he can't think about it from multiple perspectives.
Can critical thinking actually be taught? Decades of cognitive research point to a disappointing answer: not really.

The theory of transferable skills has manifested itself in many different ways: from a justification for compulsory Greek to a recommendation to lie on the grass staring at the sky. But regardless of the practical manifestation, the underlying theoretical claim is groundless.

A society where all 16-year-olds are literate is one that will still face technological disruption and political polarization, but it is one that will manage those challenges better than a society that has chased vague, ill-defined skills while neglecting the very knowledge that makes those skills possible.

t: My Leader Only Gets Sound Bites About My Performance
q: As organizations get flatter and leaders manage an increasing number of team members, staying abreast of everyone's successes and progress has become a significant challenge.
The gap between what a team member gets done and how their leader perceives that work is one of the most underrated risks in a career.

Leaders trust secondhand reports far more than self-generated ones, because they assume a personal update is self-serving. When a peer mentions in a meeting that you were the one who caught a critical mistake, or a client describes how invaluable your influence has become, that sound bite does more to promote your work than ten status reports.
The real strategy, then, isn't just managing up but managing sideways so well that other people become your PR team.
The easiest version goes something like this: 'That means a lot. Would you mind mentioning it to my leader?'

Perception management is not vanity. It's part of the job. Many high performers, especially junior ones, secretly reject the idea of shaping how they are seen, believing the work should speak for itself. It doesn't.

t: Math Class Asks Kids to Become Somebody Else
q: Students frequently feel like they have to leave essential parts of themselves at the classroom door in order to be successful in math class.

Then the student has to somehow metabolize the fact that they are marked incorrect by their teacher for answering with the exact answer and not an inexact answer. Success in this problem requires imprecision even when precision is right there. You're right if you're wrong.

Math class asks kids to disassociate from their better selves and rational instincts hundreds of times throughout a school year. Kids realize quickly that there is zero upside in asking 'okay but is there a situation where estimation is actually useful?'

The teacher is rewarded for getting the kid to estimate, not for getting the kid to inhabit themselves more fully. The teacher then treats the kid as an object in service of that project, rather than their own subject.
We can ask ourselves, 'What is a situation where estimation might feel necessary and natural? If estimation is aspirin, then what is the headache?'

This activity, like all others in our curriculum, comes from an ethic that says, 'How can we take kids as they are and build from there, to build better versions of ourselves together?' The alternative is to ask kids daily to become somebody else, to invite them to choose daily between themselves and mathematics. Their choice shouldn't surprise us.

t: Education, When AI Just Is
q: AI is embedded in our browsers, our phones, our search engines, our workplaces, and increasingly the ordinary applications through which we read, write, communicate, and make decisions. We are quickly moving beyond a world in which people consciously decide to 'use AI.' It is becoming part of the environment in which cognition happens.
What if learning no longer prepared people to participate in consequential work, but occurred through that participation itself?

If AI can produce the artifact, what evidence of learning remains? How do we move from verifying that students worked independently to revealing how they exercised judgment, agency, and integrity while working with intelligence that was not their own?

AI is increasingly designed to anticipate difficulty and remove it before we experience it. But learning science tells us that effort, uncertainty, revision, and struggle are often the very things that allow knowledge to endure. The danger is not simply that students will avoid doing work. It is that they may experience the feeling of mastery without undergoing the process through which mastery develops.

When AI is already part of students' literacy environment, is refusing to teach it an act of protection—or an abdication of teaching? Students are already reading, writing, thinking, and communicating within environments shaped by AI. Refusing to address that reality does not preserve some pre-AI form of literacy. It leaves students alone to navigate systems they have never been taught to question.

t: Your Son Is Not the Problem. His Youth Group Might Be.
q: Middle-school and high-school boys are drawn to impressive men. They are drawn to men who represent the kind of men they aspire to become. They want to be around aspirational men: men who are smart, serious, intense, rigorous, and articulate; men who will challenge them intellectually and call them to greatness in mind, body, and soul.

Most youth ministries are structured for girls, not boys. Too often, the male leaders lack the masculine gravitas, competence, and strength that adolescent boys admire. This is why the games are silly rather than demanding.

Fathers, here is the bottom line: if you are not awe-inspired by the men leading your son's youth ministry, and your son shows no interest in attending, do not force him to go. You are making it worse for everyone.

Your sons want to be around Kings, Warriors, Sages, and Lovers. The best resources for middle-school and high-school boys in the church are the other men in the church. Every church has men who have been tested in these areas and have thrived.

Boys from broken homes need a multi-generational brotherhood exponentially more than they need to play 'Cheeto Face.' Fathers, do not waste your sons' middle-school and high-school years by subjecting them to men who do not impress you.

Boys are turning to online influencers because many of those men project strength, competence, seriousness, and aspiration. Do not blame the 'manosphere' without asking why church leaders have failed to offer a more compelling model of manhood.

t: Who Is Teaching Young Men to Live?
q: For anyone paying attention, it's clear that young people, especially young men, are struggling. Many today are anxious and lonely, searching for meaning, direction, purpose… anything. Whether they know it or not, they're looking for someone who can help them figure out life.

Previous generations suffered wars, economic collapse, disease, and personal tragedy on a scale that most will never experience. Yet they didn't have on-demand therapy to talk through their problems. Instead, they relied on something else.

All these educational experiences promoted a common vision of the actualized human person. Western societies, particularly those shaped by Christianity, had a more coherent answer on what maturity meant. A good man was not simply someone who achieved personal satisfaction, but rather someone who practiced virtue, fulfilled obligations, served others, and oriented their life toward the highest good.

Therapy is the rescue operation when things have gone awry. Mentorship and formation are the way we, throughout our lives, gain the wisdom and virtues necessary to avoid falling into mental roadblocks, sins, and personal problems that require therapy.

Like Dante waking dazed in a wood, they are lacking direction. They have ambition and potential, but little vision of what to use those gifts for. Dante doesn't discover the way himself; nor does he soon discover the right way through introspection, or as we might say today by 'finding himself'. No, he must be led by a guide.

Boys are turning to online influencers because many of those men project strength, competence, seriousness, and aspiration. Do not blame the 'manosphere' without asking why church leaders have failed to offer a more compelling model of manhood.

t: The Skill That Got Me Promoted Was the One I Had to Give Up
q: Someone once told me, plainly, that the thing I was best at was the thing that would keep me from being promoted.

Sit with how that lands when you are twenty-eight and everything you are proud of is your own flawlessness. I was not being told to improve. I was being told to give up the one thing that had gotten me everything so far. It felt less like advice and more like being told the ground I was standing on was the problem.

That thought is the whole reason this is hard. In the moment you finally loosen your grip and something goes wrong, it does not feel like a lesson about growth. It feels like proof that you should never have loosened it in the first place.

If I could not let go, I could not scale. And if I could not scale, I could not lead. I would spend my whole career as the most reliable individual performer in the building, valuable and capped, doing more and more of the same work, never trusted with more, because everything I touched required me to touch it. Perfection is an individual sport.

When you check everything yourself, every error feels equally fatal. A typo and a broken model feel the same in your stomach, because your name is on all of it and you cannot tell the difference between what matters and what does not. You have no sense of proportion, because proportion is a thing you can only develop from a little distance.
It felt like losing myself. It was the beginning of actually being able to lead.

t: The Most Expensive Assumption We Ever Made
q: We called them digital natives. Their the digital generation, they just get technology or my kid knows how to use my phone better than I do. This is what many of us assumed 15 years ago when smart phones and social media started to encroach upon our daily lives. If kids were born knowing how to navigate technology, then we didn't have to teach it. We could hand them the device and step back.

What kids actually have is comfort — fast thumbs, no fear of the interface. What they don't have, unless someone teaches it, is comprehension of what the technology is doing to them and for them. Comfort and comprehension look identical from across the room. They are not the same thing, and the gap between them is exactly where a generation got hurt.

When the OECD tested fifteen-year-olds across dozens of countries on whether they could distinguish fact from opinion in what they read online, fewer than one in ten could do it reliably. These are the same students who can run three apps at once, who live on their phones, who look — from across the room — completely fluent. They could open everything. They could evaluate almost nothing.

This is the social media pattern replaying in real time. Mass adoption by kids. Minimal awareness by adults. Zero instruction in between. We have seen this exact movie, and we know the ending, and we are watching it again with the sequel.

Ask that same confident-looking student whether the answer is right, or where it came from, or what the tool quietly got wrong, or whether they should have used it at all — and you find the same gap we found with social media. They don't know that these systems generate plausible text rather than verified truth. They don't know the machine will invent a source with a straight face. Access is not understanding. It never was.
The second pillar is a refusal: don't assume fluency. Teach it. Deliberately, as curriculum, the way we would teach anything else that matters.

t: Strat Chat - Underrated Checks for Understanding
q: There's no denying, Checking for Understanding is the greatest tool a teacher has to inform them of current student performance and misconceptions developing at a whole class level. It is an avenue to create a positive feedback loop with students while also creating formative action to correct and improve upon misconceptions or incomplete responses.

The best teachers will not only check for understanding, they will have a repertoire of a small and powerful set of strategies and change the way in which they check regularly to keep things fresh for the students as well as varying whether they are required to think fast or think slow.

We can however fall into a trap that our lessons will become rigid and formulaic where students are hit with content, true/false, content, MCQ, content, think/pair/share in such a consistent order that students move from active engagement in the thinking to running on autopilot.

We know the use of examples and non-examples is a useful tool in explicit teaching and a similar logic applies here. If students understand what the answer is, we also need them to understand what the answer isn't.
Suddenly, this scenario has gone from Adam having a 50/50 chance at being correct to needing to explain his thinking in more depth.

AI tools can also be your friend in the creation of these imperfect responses as our LLM friends are able to punch out intelligent sounding nonsense both deliberately and accidentally which can be of great use for our classes.

t: Leadership Beyond Technique
q: Leadership, no less than literary education, must be animated first by a care for advancing what is most human. To organize, to operate, to levy strategic clarity is to participate in acts of love; it is to take seriously the communal implications of thoughtful order.

When reduced to technique, performance, or the mastery of professional tools, leadership loses its magnanimous purpose. It is easily forgotten in our age of systems, strategies, dashboards, and management literature that leadership is not finally justified by productivity.

A leader who cuts corners teaches that appearances matter more than integrity. A leader who avoids hard conversations teaches that false harmony is preferable to truth. A leader who praises talent but ignores character teaches that giftedness excuses disorder. A leader who is perpetually hurried teaches that people are interruptions.

Leadership reaches its proper fulfillment only when these instruments serve a deeper inheritance: when they help create a place where truth can be spoken plainly, where good work is honored, where joy is not feigned, where dignity is preserved, where standards are clear, where burdens are shared, and where others are strengthened rather than merely used.

Leadership is therefore not only directional. It is formative. In that sense, leadership bears a deep resemblance to education. The leader is always teaching, even when no formal lesson is being given.
Leadership is proven not by how much depends upon the leader, but by how much good continues to live and grow in the people and culture under his care.

t: Leaders Learn by Changing What They Notice
q: An occasional 'mind cleanse' is essential for critical and creative thinking.
Probably the most common advice for seeing things anew is for leaders to change their vantage point.
He suggests leaders should notice 'ghosts and ruins,' his words for the traces of the past that remain in place, like abandoned features or faded uses.
When leaders view matters from different personas, they focus on issues and ask the questions those roles require of them.
The idea is to interrupt entrenched habits long enough to let something true come into view.

t: I Built a Team That Could Run Without Me. Then I Found Out Why.
q: We also learned early when we could afford to hire, and we hired well. The people we brought on took real ownership of their roles, in all kinds of ways I didn't expect and couldn't have done better myself.
For a long time I told that story as proof we'd built something great. And we had. But I left out the part that actually explains it. The business was easy.

That's the trap, and it's a sneaky one. When things are easy, a team that just executes looks identical to a team that could handle anything. You genuinely cannot tell them apart on a good day. You only find out which one you built when it gets hard, and by then it's a rough time to be finding out.

Good is exactly when to hand people real problems. Not just tasks to run, but things to figure out, decisions to own, messes to sort through while the stakes are still low and you can afford for it to be a little clumsy.

The point of a team that runs without you was never that they can hold things steady when it's smooth. Anyone can do that. It's that when it gets hard, they solve it, and it doesn't all come running back to you.

I had a fabulous team. But I'd built them for good times and set ways. They were excellent at running the machine when the machine was already working. What they'd never been trained to do was solve a real problem, because for years we barely had any.

t: How Releasing Writers Completely Changed My Teaching
q: Before Releasing Writers: When we wrote, we used the curriculum organizers, which were different every single time. This meant learning a new system with every new writing assignment.

This change has significantly reduced the cognitive load on kids that usually comes with writing. This consistency also allows kids to translate the skills into any writing task, in any subject. Instead of each graphic organizer and process being specific to the prompt, they are general, so students are repeating the process over and over, internalizing the process and using them in any setting.

Before Releasing Writers: I used to hear: 'I don't know what to do next' or 'I'm stuck' all of the time. Writing can be one of the most cognitively challenging tasks for students. Between mechanics, syntax, idea production, organization, vocabulary, and the many other pieces involved in writing, when there is no consistent process or framework, students got even more overwhelmed.

Students cheer 'yes!' when I announce we are doing writing. Students who previously despised this time ask me every morning 'are we doing writing?', and it has quickly become my favorite subject to teach.
Being able to write well is something that not everyone can do. It is a huge test of synthesizing all literacy skills. It requires students to retrieve spelling, organ
Now, I don't have a sea of hands waiting for help- not only is it less overwhelming for the students, but it is for me too! Self talk also helps students feeling stuck persevere.

t: How Did the Laboratory Become the Arbiter of Learning in Classrooms?
q: It can be said that much of developmental psychology is the science of the strange behavior of children in strange situations with strange adults for the briefest periods of time" (Urie Bronfenbrenner, 1977).

Placing an individual child in strange situations, doing strange things in strange places with strange adults dressed in white coats carrying clipboards—you will have to decide for yourself whether this is the path to truth and enlightenment.

In 1979 he published his book The Ecological Model of Human Development which ushered in a new criterion for research: ecological validity. On this view, it is a mistake to believe one has found the truth about human development based on a decontextualized measurement of a behavior produced in a laboratory deliberately stripped of all other legible factors which might have influenced an outcome.

The independent variable is phonemic awareness training. The dependent variable is decoding score. The finding is a meta-analytic effect size aggregated across dozens of these studies, interpreted as a main effect: explicit phonemic awareness instruction produces better readers than business as usual. The epistemic warrant, the arbiter, is the aggregated significance test.

So what? How does one bridge the gap between the finding and the subject world we share and are interested in improving? Was Christmas a dark time of year for Little Albert from thence forward? Did the children in the Bobo doll study become more aggressive?

Determining whether direct instruction in phonemic awareness can improve decoding skills, however, is different. We do see children's great enjoyment in language play, in rhyming words, in making up sounds and words. Is it possible that direct instruction using refined protocols for manipulating phonemes could have a positive impact on decoding?

t: Five Historical Novels Every Child Should Read Before High School
q: In order for American children to understand history, they must first learn to appreciate the values, customs, and traditions of past generations. This can best be done through historical fiction, which gives students a window into places, people, and ideas that are very different from their own experiences.
Historical fiction can also pique a student's interest in a particular time period or event.
Older historical novels—particularly those written before 1970—are best at this.
These books, set respectively in the woods of Wisconsin and upstate New York, give children a glimpse into the hard work, resourcefulness, and fortitude of ordinary 19th century Americans.
Novelist L. P. Hartley wrote that 'The past is a foreign country. They do things differently there.' His statement is truer today than ever.

The accelerating change in our culture now means that even the 20th century seems alien to today's students. But good books—especially historical literature—can be a passport to the past, helping students understand and empathize with the generations of Americans that came before them.

t: Claude Is Free for Teachers. Here Are Fifteen Things I Use It For.
q: Every article about AI for teachers uses the same three examples. Write a lesson plan, draft a rubric, generate discussion questions. Save time. I understand why — they're easy to explain in a paragraph. But if that's the whole of what you've tried, and what came back was generic and needed fixing anyway, you probably concluded the thing was oversold. That's a reasonable conclusion to draw from that evidence.

I don't write careful prompts. I've read the guides on how to do it and I don't do it. What I type instead is the same half-legible note I'd scribble on the back of a folder — the drills we ran, who debated whom, the four things I want on the slides — and then I upload whatever materials I already have sitting on my computer and let it work out what I meant.

I often don't type at all. There's a microphone button in the message box and I use it constantly. I talk, it transcribes, it goes from there. A good share of the notes described below started as me talking rather than writing, including a fair amount of this post.

Almost every lesson, handout, and set of class materials I make goes into Claude before it goes to a student. Sometimes I just ask for general feedback. More often I ask something specific, and being specific is what makes it useful: will an eleven-year-old follow this, will this interest a college student, which words here are they not going to know, where does the pacing sag, is the third section trying to do too much.

The standards connection is the part that goes beyond a discount. Through Learning Commons, Claude has each state's standards along with the smaller competencies underneath them and the order students usually learn them in, so what you get back is scaffolded rather than just on topic.

I pay for Max, and I want to be plain about what that buys, because I'd rather nobody read this post and conclude they need to spend money. It buys me room and one extra model. Everything described here works on the free teacher account.

t: Beyond CUBES: Rethinking How I Teach Word Problems
q: CUBES was giving my students a procedure for what to do to the words in the problem. It wasn't necessarily giving them knowledge about the mathematical structure underneath those words.

My students could circle the numbers. They could underline the question. They could box a word. And very often, they could still have absolutely no idea whether the numbers in the problem should be added, subtracted, multiplied or divided.
On high-stakes tests, keyword strategies work <50% of the time. (Powell, Namkung, & Lin, 2022)

More signaled the student to add, but they really need to subtract. The mathematical structure of that problem never changed. Both would be considered Compare problems, in schema instruction. What changed was the location of the unknown within the problem, but the student wasn't able to recognize that, because they were focused on the key word, more, that they had learned meant to add.
Instead of teaching students to ask: What operation am I supposed to do? or: What keyword tells me what to do? we can teach them to ask: What kind of mathematical relationship is happening here?

We tend to present word problems to children as though every new story is a new problem to figure out. When really it isn't. Underneath all of the names, objects, settings, and numbers are a relatively small number of mathematical structures. Those structures are called schemas. And we can explicitly teach students to recognize them.

t: Stop Arguing Your Case. Start Holding the Question.
q: I'm going to suggest a fourth way instead. I call it holding.
Trying to argue your way to change isn't likely to work. People often don't behave like rational actors.

Ghosting is what happens when leaders realize, often after one or two failed attempts, that the communication challenge is harder than anticipated. Rather than try a third time, the leader finds some way of working around the roadblock or simply accepts the status quo.
Holding is the recognition that some problems and possibilities need to be carried in the organizational atmosphere for a while before anyone can work on them.

What Rachel actually did—without necessarily knowing it—is hold the question of whether a webinar series would be valuable for the organization. She held it in her own mind, she raised it in conversation, she brought data to it when that was appropriate, and she let it develop.

t: Some Power Games That Happen in Schools
q: From my own experience, I know that power can turn people in education into self-centred individuals.

They are no longer judged by their teaching, but by their control of the teachers who work for them and their control of the school. They are rewarded for their decisiveness even if the decision they made wasn't based on consulting teachers who were affected by it.

Power tends to change the social environment around senior leaders. People laugh at their jokes more. They stop being challenged, and often their ideas are accepted too quickly. Over time, this can create a bubble where they believe their perspective is the objective truth.
Those leaders who aren't sure about leading can often slip into power games because they are scared of what could happen if they don't step in and manage and control how staff work.

Teachers can cope with high expectations, they cope with them every day. What wears them down is the sense that the rules are not stable, and that their professional worth is being assessed through a lens they cannot control.

t: Moral Panic at the Academy
q: The Standards are poor. They are not based on evidence from cognitive science or high-quality education research. For example, they do not mention explicit teaching, cognitive load theory, the worked example effect, retrieval practice, spaced practice, or methods of checking for understanding.

There is little research evidence to support differentiation and yet it sits in the Standards while evidence-informed approaches do not. This shows the Standards are based more on ideology and romantic ideas of how the author/s would like the world to be than being based on how the world actually is.

The pernicious effect of having differentiation in the Standards is that a teacher using whole-class, explicit teaching may be seen by some as failing to differentiate. And so the evidence-blind practice defeats the evidence-informed one.

'Were they the ones that followed a pre-determined script and rigid lesson plan. Or was it an educator responsive to the young people in their care? Who adapted their approach by using a range of techniques to engage everyone in the room.'
I expect that many lecturers make some pretty disparaging remarks about this content, given it conflicts so deeply with their ideologies of teaching and education.

t: Leave Jason Arday Alone – This Is a Scandal of Academic Educational Leadership
q: Jason Arday absolutely doesn't deserve all the nasty criticism. He was a young scholar trying to make his way, and like lots of us but more so, made huge mistakes in search of the prize of a successful academic career.

The real significance of the Arday case is that it serves as a further demonstration that the field of educational academia has lost a sense of its primary, substantive purpose: to generate and share knowledge that will improve education.

This managerialism has perverse consequences. Not only is research judged against spurious measures of quality and impact, but academia is judged against broader social metrics, including those related to diversity and inclusion, that may very well serve to distract from or supersede academic issues.
The leaders in the field do not seem to be interested in putting the field back on track—they are more concerned with following what is strategically useful to maintaining their status.

Hattie and Arday are both stars valuable to the reputation of the university, so they were protected. In both cases, the important aspect is not related to the specific research agenda, but to political usefulness for the institution.

t: I Finally Got My Kid a Phone
q: We are firm believers in giving kids as much freedom as they can handle.

I've seen how kids text message each other and I think it's a shame. So much is lost in translation and frankly I think we all do ourselves a disservice when we default to texting. Calling gives so much information on tone, emotion, intent, and is also quicker than texting and more human because it is synchronous.
This phone is plugged into the wall in the living room. No texting. No screen—no browsers, no social media, nothing to worry about.
Asked Claude Fable how to configure it. Follow the instructions. Takes about 30 minutes.
Please buy your kid a regular phone so other kids can call them.

t: Getting Ready for a Better Conversation and a Deeper Relationship
q: Without an ongoing conversation, relationships don’t exist. People enact relationships one conversation at a time.
Now for some intuitive wisdom: If a leader wants to strengthen or deepen a relationship, they must change the conversation.
Relationships and conversations that get stuck in small talk remain mostly superficial.
Sharing a real opinion means taking a small risk together. This is what starts to build deeper trust and connection.
If the conversation defines any relationship, then improving it isn’t a soft skill. It’s the whole job.

t: From Confusion to Clarity: Creating Common Expectations for AI Use
a: Jennifer W. Shewmaker and Julie Crum
q: The challenge isn't that teachers approach AI differently but that students are left trying to decode a brand-new set of rules every time they change classes.

Students aren't always asking, 'How do I do this assignment?' More often they're wondering, 'Am I allowed to use AI for this? If so, how can I use it?' That's mental energy we want them investing in learning, not in guessing about expectations.

The real leadership challenge of the AI era—providing enough structure for both teachers and students so there is clarity rather than fear while allowing room for the flexibility needed for different fields, levels of learning, and learning outcomes.
Policies alone, however, don't always translate into clear expectations on an ordinary weekday morning. Too often, students discover the boundaries only after they've crossed them.

A principle we've been emphasizing at Lipscomb is that clarity supports learning. The important thing is that students understand the expectations before they begin an assignment, not after they've unintentionally crossed a line.

t: 628. Listen To Lead
q: Listening, when done with intention, sends a clear message: 'I value your perspective.' That simple acknowledgment can build trust more profoundly and more quickly than even the most inspiring speech.

'We need to teach people to listen...That is the biggest revolution we realized, that we don't know how to listen, okay? We're taught to speak, and we're taught to debate, but we're not taught to listen.' —Bob Chapman
'You cannot learn if you cannot listen. Listening produces clearer thinking and better ideas and greater motivation for action, and that dramatically expands what we can achieve.' —David Novak
'Speak confidently as if you are right but listen carefully as if you are wrong.' —Kevin Kelly

Active listening helps leaders recognize emerging challenges early, before they become more serious. By understanding the nuances behind concerns, frustrations, or inefficiencies, leaders can respond with insight and agility.

t: Your AI Policy Is a Rule, and Students Route Around Rules
q: A list of prohibitions teaches a student how to hide, not how to work.

A student who asks the bot to write the argument skips the exact struggle where learning lives. A student who writes the argument first and then asks the bot to attack it has to defend it or rethink it. It's the same tool, but one of those students got smarter.
So stop writing rules about AI and start writing the workflow. Do the thinking first, then let the machine pressure it.

A student who writes 'I used AI on this' has told you nothing. A student who writes 'I asked ChatGPT to outline counterarguments, then wrote and rejected two of them myself' has told you where she leaned and where she worked.
If honesty about AI use costs points, you have taught your class that hiding it is the correct strategy. They are very good at strategy.
Set it per assignment, not per course. 'AI allowed' across fifteen weeks means nothing when week three is a reflection and week eleven is a data analysis.

t: Why Every Christian Should Read Old Books
q: St. Augustine spent years immersed in Cicero, Virgil, and the Latin classics before becoming one of Christianity's greatest theologians.

'This book of his contains an exhortation to philosophy...But this book altered my affections, and turned my prayers to Thyself, O Lord; and made me have other purposes and desires. Every vain hope at once became worthless to me; and I longed with an incredibly burning desire for an immortality of wisdom.'
Augustine eventually rejected Cicero's philosophy where it conflicted with Christianity, but he never rejected the pursuit of wisdom that Cicero had inspired.

Within their scriptoria, monks copied not only the Scriptures but also the writings of Aristotle, Plato, Virgil, Ovid, Livy, Tacitus, Cicero, and countless other authors whose works might otherwise have disappeared.

'Just as dyers prepare the cloth before they apply the dye...so indeed must we also, if we would preserve indelible the idea of the true virtue, become first initiated in the pagan lore, then at length give special heed to the sacred and divine teachings.'

The Church Fathers read the great books of the ancient world with open eyes and careful judgment. They neither idolized them nor discarded them. They received what was true, rejected what was false, and allowed the best of classical wisdom to serve the higher light of the Gospel.

t: Who's Really Teaching Helplessness?
q: There's a common criticism that explicit instruction creates learned helplessness by providing too much support. But if learned helplessness is the belief that your efforts won't lead to success, we should ask a different question. Who's really teaching helplessness?
Learned helplessness is not produced by too much support. It is produced by repeated failure with no path to success.

Sometimes we throw students into the deep end in the name of independence and watch them flounder. Other times, convinced they'll never be able to access the core curriculum, we lower the bar altogether and replace meaningful learning with tasks designed simply to keep them occupied. Both approaches teach the same lesson: this isn't for you.
True independence is not the absence of instruction. It is what happens after good instruction.
The goal of scaffolding is always eventual removal—but the removal has to be earned by demonstrated mastery, not imposed prematurely by ideology.

t: What Makes a Teacher: Everything I Wish I Learned in College
q: Nobody ever said the word dyslexia. Not once. Not in a single one of those genuinely science-based, best-practice reading courses.

Schools of education should teach dyslexia. Period. It is a reading disability that affects as many as one in five students, which means there is no version of a teaching career where you don't encounter it.

Leaving future teachers uneducated about what dyslexia is and how to address it as a tier one practitioner is the equivalent of the medical field declining to train OBGYNs in perimenopause and menopause care.

I was placed in a 6th grade classroom with 38 students. My cooperating teacher was burnt out beyond belief, and her friend stated bluntly that I had been assigned to help her. I wasn't there to learn. I was there to be a second adult in the room.

The more years I teach, the more convinced I become that we've built teacher preparation programs all wrong. Not just in what is taught, which is the loudest complaint these days, but in how they're structured.
Year two is student teaching, and nothing else. No additional coursework beyond protected time to sit with a master teacher one on one and actually learn the job.

t: The Reading Crisis Is Neither New Nor Inevitable
q: The reality is that the notion of a crisis of reading is neither new nor inevitable. As K-12 educators know, we've been teaching and learning amidst 'A Nation at Risk' for decades now, and the crisis framing has long preceded that.
On any given day, only two percent of American adults read to a child.

As a school leader, doing something about 'the end of reading' requires pushing back on the status quo. It requires cultivating a culture within your community that reinforces that reading matters and celebrates why it matters.

The way you organize the physical space within your school speaks volumes. Ask yourself, what would each space in my school community look like if it were impossible to miss that this is a school that is invested in reading and literacy?

Invest first in what I'd consider the most critical part of intellectual preparation—our own understanding of the texts, what's meaningful about them, and why they matter. Start your next planning meeting with teachers by asking, 'What did you love (or hate!) about this text?'

As Octavia Butler once wrote, 'there's no single answer that will solve all of our future problems. There's no magic bullet. Instead there are thousands of answers—at least. You can be one of them if you choose to be.'

t: The Downside of Using Exclusion to Create Group Cohesion
q: Somewhat ironically, excluding people often creates a deeper connection and more pride in being a member. Exclusion is one of the oldest tricks in the leadership playbook, and it's worth understanding exactly how and why it works.
Nothing bonds a group faster than rejecting others or celebrating a shared sense of being chosen. That's why exclusion is so tempting for leaders in a hurry to increase group cohesion.

Over time, people start to fear being rejected by the group and excluded like the outsiders they've been taught to look down on. So, they fall in line. They become less willing to speak up about issues they disagree with, because disagreement begins to feel like disloyalty.
The very cohesion that felt so strong at the start slowly turns brittle. It holds together through fear of exclusion rather than genuine commitment.
Good leaders create belonging without making it dependent on exclusion. They resist the shortcut of an 'us' versus 'them' story, even though it is fast and effective.
The circle that holds people by fear will always be weaker than the one that holds them by choice.

t: The Alpha School Debate
q: Alpha School and its parent company, 2-Hour Learning, argue that the tired, inefficient era of 'a teacher standing in front of a classroom' must come to an end.

Jared Cooney Horvath is doubtful that success with an AI-assisted tutor, or on tests that mimic that situation, will transfer to other learning contexts. Robert Pondiscio questions Alpha's confident, even arrogant tone and points out they haven't made their underlying data available for review by independent third parties.
Dylan Kane notes that learning via a screen is fundamentally different from human-powered instruction; for example, studies have shown that reading on screens results in weaker comprehension.

Paul Kirschner agrees with all of the above and adds that academic subjects shouldn't be viewed as 'just administrative hurdles that kids have to clear before their real education and learning can begin.'

My sense is that AI-assisted tutoring works best for math, and maybe science, where learning proceeds in a more clearly hierarchical, sequential fashion. With literature or history, the sequence of learning isn't as clear, and the universe of concepts to be learned is far less finite.
Several people have questioned whether Alpha's model would work with students from less affluent and highly educated families. Tuition at Alpha can run as high as $75,000 a year.

t: Rites of Passage
q: I traded my guitar for a gun and spent months crawling in the dirt in Southern California alongside hundreds of other young men who were intent on becoming United States Marines.
The pain in bootcamp is mundane. If you're in decent shape, it's not a problem. What is much more thorough and impactful, however, is the sustained humiliation.
Humiliation is like a good marinade before searing the meat. It makes it pliable for the work to come.

You have no first name and if you find yourself having to communicate with a drill instructor, you must only use the third person to refer to yourself. There is no 'self' now...just another Marine recruit among many.

Any infraction is rewarded with physical pain and degradation, and sometimes an added psychological element if you do something stupid: you might have to write letters to your fellow recruits' mothers, wives, and children to explain why your selfishness, incompetence, weakness, or stupidity has caused their son, husband, or father to die unnecessarily.

To succeed in this environment requires negotiating a sustainable truce between your fear of pain and humiliation, your resentment at being forced into those feelings, your own disgust with yourself for feeling them in the first place, and a prudent management of your physical capacity for suffering.

t: Modeling K-12 After Northeastern University and Link Ventures
q: 'Our whole model is geared up for young, but now we're talking about another level of young. We have some thinking to do.'

Schools know how to manage students this young—it is the one thing they indisputably know—but not founders. The fund knows founders—the capital, the mentors, the network, the path from pitch to company—but not fourteen-year-olds.
Here is what American secondary education spent the last two years arguing about while a fourteen-year-old trained a foundation model: where students may keep their phones.

He calls the reflex what it is: 'our first reaction was a protectionist reaction,' built on 'the students will be cheating.' And he goes further: higher education 'divorced ourselves from the real world.'
Same kid, same laptop—one institution sees a discipline problem, the other sees a founder.

t: Jim Callaghan's Secret Garden, Fifty Years On
q: It is known as the 'Secret Garden' speech because Callaghan compared the world of education to a secret garden that elected politicians, parents and ordinary taxpayers were not allowed to have an opinion on, even when things were obviously going wrong.

Even that circumlocutory phrasing was inflammatory, and was enough to bring out the 'continental tyranny' counter argument: the general secretary of the head teachers' union compared the proposal to Nazi interference in the 1930s German curriculum.

Callaghan's speech was just a speech, and wasn't followed up by any legislation on curriculum. It was enormously influential and was frequently cited 12 years later when the Conservative government passed the landmark 1988 Education Reform Act.
It was always going to be unsustainable for education to receive so much funding from central government, but for central government to have so little say over it.

The lesson from the past is that if you devolve power and responsibility without commensurate tax-raising powers, you get problems. You risk getting irresponsible local authorities, and a meddlesome central government.

t: Every Decision Is a Prediction
q: Every map does two jobs. The first is explaining what you've already seen. The second is predicting what you haven't seen yet. People judge maps by the first. Reality judges them by the second.

You hire someone. Sitting across from them, you are making a claim: this person handles the work, and six months from now I'll be glad I picked them. That's a prediction with a date attached, and you almost certainly never say it out loud.
Reality answers, constantly, and faster than most people notice.
Without a prediction, an outcome is just something that happened. With a prediction, the same outcome becomes feedback.

That's how you and Dana can sit through identical months and walk out holding opposite conclusions, both of you honest. Neither of you was scoring anything, and impressions bend toward whatever you believed in January.

t: "Fixed it."
q: All I had was a question: Why do we think the managers are the problem?
She realized they'd done what harried leadership teams often do—saw a problem, latched onto a plausible explanation, and moved to solve it without testing the assumption.
Training was the catch-all solution to just about every organizational ill—usually before anyone had fully examined the issue.

When a problem arises, people naturally reach for the most visible cause so they can quickly move from uncertainty to action. Then they can declare it handled without uncovering any deeper, decidedly more inconvenient realities.
All the time and money in the world won't help you if you're solving the wrong problem or targeting the wrong cause.
I went into that leadership meeting fully expecting a smackdown. I came out with a rule I used for the rest of my career: question the diagnosis before deciding on a treatment.

t: What I Got Wrong About Pupil Progress Meetings
q: I deluded myself into thinking that I was doing 'decision driven data collection' by thinking: What improvements do we need to make to curriculum / pedagogy / interventions / operations?' and then using standardised test data to help with that decision making. In fact, I was still doing 'data driven decision making'.

Standardised tests are not an assessment of our curriculum. Reading extracts would only match the texts that we've taught by an incredible fluke and although maths tests are written to sample the national curriculum, they're incredibly unlikely to match what we've taught either.

At the time, I thought that using standardised test scores was the right thing to do because it was the most reliable assessment and would allow for the most valid of inferences by virtue of the standardisation and benchmarking against national comparison; a perfect example of misunderstanding the data and using it for something it isn't designed for.

Turns out that none of that was necessary for teachers to talk about the common or individual barriers to greater success. The reality was that the meetings were more for leaders than they were for teachers. We wanted to know how children were doing and contribute to making improvements but we were taking up teachers' time using inadequate information to do it.

meetings yield actions for leaders. This is particularly important if there are obvious patterns in what barriers exist and a common need for certain strategies. If either are systemic, it is leaders' job to tackle it. Even if barriers are not systemic, it is still our responsibility to support and enable colleagues to improve on an individual basis.

Until recently, our model for pupil progress meetings was a termly conversation with a year group at a time. We'd use progress matrices that showed KS1 attainment against the most recent standardised test score in reading and maths as a starting point for identifying children that might need more than we're providing. They'd result in adaptations to curriculum, pedagogy, intervention and operations.

t: Three Tenses of Sense Giving
q: The role of leadership for collective sense making is sense giving; guiding the team to interpret events and situations in a way that makes action towards educational goals more likely or more cohesive. This is not telling people what to think or presenting a narrow account of events.

Sense making is inherently retrospective; something happens and we seek to understand it: a set of academic results, patterns of pastoral incidents, fluctuating numbers on roll etc. But leaders need to look ahead, attempting predictions of future states to prepare the school for possible changes, or to paint a picture of a future desirable state.

The sense giving competency of navigating the present is challenging because it requires sense giving while the picture is still forming. But it is therefore a good opportunity to help the team to embrace ambiguity and uncertainty. It requires vulnerability but that in turn can help to develop trusting relationships.

Change work is not school improvement in the conventional sense. It is not a programme, a strategy document or an initiative. Change work is architectural. It decides where judgement lives, how risk is carried and which problems the system will stop manufacturing.

If we don't frame the past, we risk leaving successes unattributed and challenges unacknowledged, both of which are crucial to develop institutional memory. If we don't navigate the present, the team will make sense of what is happening and why from multiple, narrow viewpoints and risk fragmented decision making. If we don't inspire the future, we may remain perpetually reactive, leaving us poorly prepared for increasingly challenging times.
The beauty of narrative is that it can provide a structure for sense giving over tenses.

t: The Best Case Fallacy
q: If we always look on the bright side of life then we fall into 'the best case fallacy'. In Scruton's words, this leads inexorably to "a kind of addiction to unreality that informs the most destructive forms of optimism: a desire to cross out reality, as the premise from which practical reason begins, and to replace it with a system of compliant illusions.
Unscrupulous optimism doesn't just distort our private decisions; it shapes public policy, institutional reform and billion dollar procurement programmes.
We routinely launch new policies, spend money on new systems, train teachers in trendy-sounding pedagogical gimmickry and almost never run pilot programmes, or have a clear evaluation plan in place.

Without such an honest and critical appraisal of our efforts we're gambling with children's futures. And the problem with gamblers is that they don't actually see themselves as risk-takers. They convince themselves that they can beat the odds, that they've discovered a fool-proof system to buck the odds.

Judicious pessimism teaches us not to idolise human beings, but to forgive them their faults and to strive in private for their amendments. It teaches us to limit our ambitions in the public sphere, and to keep open the institutions, customs and procedures whereby mistakes are corrected and faults confessed to, rather than aim for some new arrangement in which mistakes are never made.

Complex systems don't fail because individuals behave badly but because ordinary people respond predictably to the incentives the system creates. To hope that everyone will exercise restraint is a wager against human nature, and history suggests it's a very poor bet.

t: The Art of Disagreement
q: And here is what almost every leader gets wrong about disagreement. You were taught to treat it as a process for finding the right answer. In the decisions that matter most, there is often no single right answer available at the moment you must decide, and pretending otherwise is how organisations talk themselves into false confidence.

When two capable, well-informed people reach opposite conclusions from the same evidence, it is usually because the thing itself is uncertain, not because one of them has reasoned badly. The disagreement is a property of the decision, not a defect in the person you are disagreeing with.

If you believe the argument should produce truth, then whoever fails to persuade you is wrong, or obstructive, or protecting something. That is precisely how the STAAR fight turned personal, with each side eventually questioning the other's motives rather than their reasoning.
A board that always votes unanimously is not necessarily aligned. It may simply have learned that dissent is unwelcome, and the cost of that lesson is invisible until something goes badly wrong.

The most dangerous version of dissent is the kind expressed in corridors and side conversations. It carries all the cost of division and none of the benefit, because the decision never gets tested by it.

A well-run disagreement is fast, because it is bounded. The positions are defined, the counter-case is evaluated, the uncertainty is stated, and then somebody decides. What actually slows organisations down is the objection nobody voiced that surfaces three months later, the executive who never really agreed and withholds effort, or the decision that gets relitigated because it was never properly argued the first time.

t: My Fraction Stories
q: A 'story,' to me, is a kind of pedagogical back-of-the-napkin sketch—an outline of a 'complete thought,' instructionally. It is not a lesson; it is less complicated and no student will see it.
Almost no students are immune to difficulties with fractions and for many students, year after year, they remain a significant obstacle. So something in and/or around the fraction story is busted.
We should not say that fractions are 'just hard'; we should see if making the story simpler will help.

Fractions are introduced to us as foreign and alien. A new family has moved into town, the Fractions, and boy are they strange—less is more but also more is more, they're always in pairs, they have weird names, strange rules and customs.
Why not give students 3/1 + 6/1 = [ ] and let them see that those strange customs aren't strange at all—you follow them yourself?

t: The next literacy challenge: Teaching students how to write
q: Writing is the last bastion of education," said Randy Barth, CEO of SRSD Online, which trains teachers in the "science of writing," encompassing a growing body of research on effective writing instruction. "Writing, I would say, is the last thing that the education system is putting money towards.
I just assumed writing instruction was happening, but every time I walk into a classroom my assumption is proven wrong," said Truckenmiller.
We have this knowledge base concentrated in a really small number of people that hasn't been scaled yet," said Truckenmiller, from Michigan State University.
Last year we were all scared of writing prompts," Arya said. "This year, we felt like we were ready.
America has not released nationwide standardized writing scores from elementary school grades since 2002, when 27 percent of fourth graders scored proficient or higher.

t: Should Self-Help Books Belong in the ELA Classroom?
q: Most of the books I studied in English class told stories about people trying to live. Many of the books I began reading later tried to tell me how to live.
A novel can remain unresolved in the mind for years. It can grow alongside us, revealing something different each time we return to it.

A self-help or professional-development book is, among other things, an argument. The author identifies a problem, proposes an explanation, and recommends a response. The book may use data, expert testimony, personal stories, historical examples, analogies, case studies, emotional appeals, or some unstable mixture of all six.
Students will encounter these claims whether schools prepare them or not. The question is whether they will learn to treat advice as something to be examined, or merely as something to accept,

Perhaps students should learn to read stories deeply and advice skeptically. They should be able to appreciate language, follow an argument, question an author, test a claim, revise their judgment, and decide what deserves to become part of their lives.
Maybe the better question is whether students should graduate knowing how to evaluate the advice that will inevitably try to shape them.
What might change if students left English class able not only to identify a theme, but also to examine a piece of advice before allowing it to become one of the themes of their lives?

t: RACI x Systems Thinking
q: You can’t mandate a system into changing. You can only change how it behaves one decision, one team, one conversation at a time and hope the pattern holds long enough to become the new normal.
People don’t play assigned roles just because a document says so. Buy-in has to be built, and it has to be built at the level where the actual decision lives, not declared from three layers up.

Clarify the specific goal before assigning roles. Co-create the RACI with the people who’ll live with it. Write out what “accountable” and “responsible” actually mean in behavioral terms, because half the time people in the same room are using the words differently.

acceptance isn’t a decision anyone makes once. It happens when a new way of thinking gets “anchored in organizational communication and continuously reproduced in everyday work.” Not approved. Reproduced. Repeatedly, locally, until it’s just how people talk to each other.

Neither of these findings is really about RACI or about automotive project management. They’re about the same underlying mechanism showing up in a governance tool and in a cultural framework: systems don’t change because someone at the top declares a new state. Change happens because a local pattern gets repeated with enough fidelity, in enough places, that it becomes the system’s new default behavior.

Global order is an emergent property of local rules, not something imposed from outside the system. What’s useful about lining up an HBR governance article with a systemic-PM academic paper is that you get the same mechanism validated in two completely different registers: hard-nosed management consulting on one side, systems-theory academic research on the other. When practitioners and theorists converge on the same answer from different directions, that’s usually a sign the answer is actually right, not just fashionable.
Holistic change was never the alternative to local iteration. It’s what local iteration looks like once you’re standing far enough back to see the whole system doing it consistently.

t: Parental Choice Is Sending Public Schools a Message. Are They Listening? ening/
q: West Virginia Board of Education President Paul Hardesty recently put the new reality plainly: Public schools are "competing for enrollment, whether we want to believe it or not.

policymakers should resist the temptation to explain the homeschool boom away as a pandemic artifact, a lifestyle preference, or a purely ideological choice. In North Carolina, many parents are saying something much more direct: The public school system is not the best place for my child.
If we're going to be the first choice for families, then we need to understand why some families are choosing not to send their kids to us.

The best public school leaders are not hiding from school choice; they're learning from it. They are building new public options, highlighting pathways families may not know about, and creating better channels for parent voice.

If families are saying that the public school system does not work for them, system leaders should seize the opportunity to ask why, study the answers, and use what they learn to become more accommodating, more receptive, and more accessible to the families they hope to serve.

t: Leadership Lessons from the Tracks
q: The best leaders don’t plan for the ideal scenario; they plan for the realistic one.

Two weeks in close quarters means tension shows up in tone and silence long before it shows up in words. When someone goes quiet at breakfast or when a “I’m fine” has an edge to it. The leaders who keep teams together are the ones who spot this early, not to fix everything, but to notice it’s there.

You don’t build trust with a new team through a mission statement, you build it by solving small, shared problems together. Maybe that’s a missed connection, an unreliable booking, or a “where do we eat now?” Every minor logistical crash is actually a trust-building opportunity in disguise.

The groups who hold their plans loosely tend to have a better time than the ones defending the original spreadsheet at all costs and good leadership is knowing when the plan has served its purpose and when it’s time to evolve it.

The reality is that we can’t control eighteen trains but we can control how we respond when the eighteenth one is cancelled. This is the skill that transfers most directly from work to travel and to pretty much everywhere else: the gap between what happens and how we react is where leadership actually lives.
The groups that come home closer aren’t the ones who never clash, they’re the ones who repair quickly instead of letting it fester into day nine of the silent treatment.

Small celebrations hold a group together more than people realise. A great meal, the view from the train window or that moment when all the preparation came together and saying it out loud matters because teams (and travel groups) run better on shared recognition than they do on gritted-teeth endurance.

None of this is really about travel. It’s about what happens when you put people together who may get on but haven’t been tested by each other yet and then ask them to make a hundred small decisions under mild logistical chaos for two weeks straight. That’s still leadership, it’s just not usually with a rucksack.

t: If Children Were Angels https://www.educationnext.org/if-children-were-angels-the-science-of-discipline-book-review-maynard/
q: The work of schooling has always involved cultivating the former in students while restraining the latter. Any theory of discipline that forgets or denies this begins in sentimentality and often ends in disorder.
The central question of school discipline cannot be what makes adults feel humane. It must be what best serves children over time.
A discipline system is instructive not only in what it says to the child who misbehaves but in what everyone else learns from watching the adults respond.

The central task of discipline, then, is not endless negotiation over rules nor therapeutic management of every conflict. It is the formation of identity through coherent norms and shared expectations.
The concern is that contemporary discipline discourse has become so focused on explaining behavior that it has lost confidence in forming it.

t: Don't Teach Students 'How to Think,' Teach Them What Is True ch_them_what_is_true_1196087.html
q: Critical thinking teaches students to evaluate evidence, identify logical fallacies, and assess arguments. These are worthwhile skills, but they are reactive.
Popularized by Paulo Freire in Pedagogy of the Oppressed, critical consciousness teaches students to interpret society primarily through relationships of power and oppression.
A free society therefore requires more than students capable of analyzing arguments; it requires citizens formed in the truths that sustain liberty.

Critical pedagogy is already teaching students how to think. It teaches them which questions to ask, which assumptions to examine, and which moral framework to adopt before evidence is ever considered.
This is why the slogan "Don't teach children what to think, teach them how to think" is not a solution — it is a surrender. The Left has already seized the "how.

t: Do Students Still Need to Learn Calculus?
q: Calculus is the gateway to almost everything we have invented in the last century, to the technology that powers the world, and to the large language models to which many people appear willing to surrender their cognition and humanity.

Math, like reading, is a muscle that must be intentionally developed. You first build the cognitive routines so that when the child gets to more advanced topics, he spends minimal time thinking about the addition, multiplication, or factorization they require.
Part of the value proposition of public education must be to provide access to the hard stuff. Calculus is demanding, and that's a good thing.
If schools instead send a message to students and parents that calculus is unimportant, they will effectively relegate most kids who heed it to working for the ones who took calculus anyway.

These twin challenges of learning loss layered on an already eroding system comprise the true educational emergency for this generation, for the next, and for all who will one day enroll their child in American public schools.

t: Contrary to Common Belief, The Poorest School Districts Outspend The Wealthiest end-the-wealthiest/
q: The findings "raise questions about what I see as a predominant narrative that local property tax finance means that poor schools don't have as much money and that that is a core, structural cause of inequality, and I just think it's not," said Sarah Reber, a senior fellow in economic studies at Brookings and the report's lead author.

They found that spending allocations across these five poverty brackets is U-shaped, with the poorest and wealthiest districts spending the most. Since the early 2000s, the poorest districts have outspent even the wealthiest ones.

The state dictates how much money school districts will receive from the state, and also what the tax policy is for how much you can raise from local taxes," said Sibilia, who is now the executive director of EdFund, a national education research and advocacy nonprofit.

Obviously, there's places that are spending much less and not really getting demonstrably worse outcomes," she said. "I think it's important to try and learn from that and try to figure out what the barriers to being more productive with spending are.

A large body of previous research has looked at differences in spending within states, but in Reber's work she found that the differences across states swamp all of this within-state difference that gets so much attention.

Many of us are returning to the "classical" education that existed for more than a thousand years prior to the progressive revolution. What did we call classical education before 1890? Simply, education.

What in the world does classical Christian education have to do with Africa? What Africans really need is training in farming. All I see on the news are famines across Africa. q: Near transfer occurs when learning is applied to a new situation that closely resembles the one in which it was acquired. The underlying structure, environment, and goals are the largely same - only minor details change.

Far transfer occurs when learning is successfully applied to a situation that differs substantially from the original learning context. While the underlying principles remain consistent, the structure, environment, and goals may all have changed.

As any educator can attest, transfer - even relatively near transfer - is one of the greatest challenges in learning. It is remarkably common for students to perform well in one setting yet struggle to apply that same knowledge in another.

This is precisely why (as discussed in our previous post) effective curricula deliberately vary the way students encounter new ideas. Rather than practicing one type of problem repeatedly in one context, students explore the same underlying concept through different modes (writing, speaking, acting), different media (textbooks, whiteboards, flashcards), different environments (the classroom, the laboratory, field trips), and different instructional approaches (explicit instruction, hands-on demonstrations, group discussions).
From Pressey’s teaching machine to brain training to AI tutors, the promise has remained the same: master the program, and that mastery will generalize to the wider world.

The major point here isn’t that students can’t learn from digital tutors – they clearly can. It’s that the learning they produce is often more contextualized, less durable, and less transferable than knowledge developed through more traditional pedagogies. Equally important, where and how we measure learning matters enormously: the closer an assessment resembles the learning environment, the more likely it is to overestimate what students have actually learned.
Put simply, the effectiveness of any digital tutor cannot be separated from the transfer demands of the assessment used to evaluate it.
Ultimately, the true test of learning is not what students can do with the tutor - but what they can still do without it.

t: The Hidden Curriculum for Adults: Why School Norms Shape Teachers More Than Policies
q: Schools spend enormous amounts of time writing policies that describe how people should behave. Yet, as Doug Lemov argues, norms almost always prove more influential than rules because they shape behaviour beneath conscious awareness. They are “largely invisible and unconscious,” yet often override formal policies because they determine what people come to regard as normal.

In the first, the dominant conversations revolve around workload, difficult pupils and the latest educational initiative that “will all be forgotten by Christmas.” Professional reading is treated with affectionate suspicion. Teachers who leave before five o’clock are jokingly referred to as “part-timers”, while martyrdom enjoys an oddly elevated social status.

If the prevailing norm suggests that asking for help signals weakness, teachers will quietly struggle alone. If staying until seven o’clock becomes synonymous with commitment, workload will expand to fill the available time. If perfectionism becomes the unofficial measure of professionalism, exhaustion slowly acquires the status of virtue.

Rather than repeatedly telling teachers that collaboration matters, make collaboration visible. Rather than encouraging wellbeing, allow respected colleagues to leave at sensible times without apology. Rather than celebrating resilience, celebrate sustainability.

Perhaps that is the most important lesson of all. Every school is constantly teaching its staff what professionalism looks like, whether intentionally or accidentally. The question is not whether norms exist - they always do. The question is whether we are shaping them deliberately or merely inheriting them from the loudest voices in the room.
