We constantly seek cues about the behaviours that signal membership. The question is rarely, What do I personally believe is best? It is far more often, What do people like me do around here?

Perhaps this also explains why leaders so often struggle to change culture through persuasion alone. We explain the rationale. We share the evidence. We produce beautifully formatted implementation plans. Yet if heuristics guide much of human behaviour automatically, leadership becomes less about convincing people and more about shaping environments in which desirable behaviours become the obvious behaviours.

When experienced teachers openly admit uncertainty, psychological safety begins to grow. Edmondson’s (1999) research demonstrates that teams learn more effectively when individuals feel safe enough to acknowledge mistakes, ask questions and seek feedback without fear of embarrassment. Likewise, Barsade’s (2002) work on emotional contagion reminds us that emotions spread rapidly through organisations. Cynicism is contagious, but luckily, so are optimism, generosity and trust.

Every school is constantly teaching its staff what professionalism looks like, whether intentionally or accidentally. The question is not whether norms exist - they always do. The question is whether we are shaping them deliberately or merely inheriting them from the loudest voices in the room. t: Leaders Who Are Difficult to Shock
q: While many leaders pride themselves on being decisive, some of the best leaders prize being measured. They cultivate a reputation for being difficult to surprise, fluster, or jolt.

When surprised, they pause before answering and do their best to separate their initial emotional reaction from the appropriate organizational response. Over time, they garner a reputation for being hard to rattle and difficult to shock.

Just as visible alarm spreads through an organization and infects morale, visible calm spreads too. When people interact with a leader who refuses to become agitated, flustered, or reactive, they stop bracing and start problem-solving.

Calm leaders make it safer for people to voice views that might be unpopular or controversial. Calm evenness isn’t merely a style. It becomes an information channel, one that keeps hard truths and unpopular opinions flowing upward so leaders can make quality decisions informed by a full range of viewpoints.

Psychologist Sigal Barsade, whose research on emotional contagion in groups helped establish the phenomenon, found that a leader’s mood spreads through a team and shapes how team members think and behave toward one another. Because composed leaders are seen as safe to challenge, they tend to hear more dissenting views and earlier warnings. This is precisely the information leaders need to make good decisions — and the kind of information that anxious teams often suppress.

Leaders who never seem to react, even to good news, risk being perceived as indifferent rather than composed. Good leaders show their emotions, just not reflexively to negative information. If a team scores a huge win and the leader’s expression doesn’t change, the team doesn’t feel steadied.

The best leaders don’t suppress what they feel. They manage the gap between feeling it and showing it. The pause before responding is where composure gets built, one surprise at a time, until it becomes a reputation.

t: The Art of Foresight
q: Foresight is not prediction. Prediction is trying to guess what will happen: who wins the election, where interest rates land, which product takes off. Prediction is mostly a mug’s game, and leaders who stake their strategy on specific predictions usually get burned.
Foresight is different. Foresight is pattern recognition applied to structural changes that are already in motion but have not yet impacted in your results.

The structural changes that will reshape your industry over the next decade are almost always visible today, if you know how to look. They are just not yet urgent, which is precisely why most firms ignore them.
The most valuable foresight rarely comes from analysing the same variables as your competitors more skilfully. It comes from noticing a change that sits outside the frame everyone else is using.
Foresight is disciplined, not fashionable. It means committing to a small number of deep structural changes and building around them for years, not lurching toward whatever is trending this month.

If your firm is not exercising foresight, someone else will exercise it on your behalf. A regulator. An investor. An acquirer. A government. And you will spend the next decade executing someone else’s judgement about your future.

You do not need a crystal ball. You need the discipline to identify the deep currents that are already flowing in your own industry, and the courage to build for where they lead, even when the destination is not yet visible in your results.

A family, school, church, or workplace should not assume that virtue will automatically grow from messages alone. People need structured learning that helps them (a) understand what a skill looks like, (b) practice it successfully, and (c) apply it across time and contexts.

t: Human Beings vs AI: Do We Have Any Lasting Advantage?

t: Rehearsal Is More Than Role Play
q: Somewhere along the way, role play has become almost synonymous with rehearsal. The two are often used interchangeably, even though one is just a particular way of rehearsing.

Nobody expects a concert pianist to prepare by simply playing the whole piece over and over again. They isolate difficult passages. They slow them down. They practise finger patterns, dynamics and transitions before stitching everything back together.
The irony is that adaptive expertise depends on routine expertise. Teachers can only adapt effectively when the fundamentals no longer demand their attention.

What will you do if only three students understand the explanation? What if almost everyone gets the hinge question wrong? These aren't hypothetical distractions. They're the moments that define teaching. Rehearsing them develops professional judgement.

I wonder whether we also need a richer vocabulary. At the moment, rehearsal often means one thing. But perhaps we should be talking about verbal rehearsal, decision rehearsal, mental rehearsal, fluency rehearsal and interactive rehearsal.

t: Overcoming Animosity Toward a Team Member
q: Without necessarily meaning to, leaders sometimes hold a grudge. They can let their negative impressions and feelings toward a team member influence how they engage with them.
The good news is that fixing it doesn’t require the team member to change at all. Animosity is a deep-seated dislike or resentment toward another person.
Learning how to overcome this feeling is essential to effective leadership. The first is a discrete event where the leader feels deeply wronged, betrayed, deceived, humiliated, or rejected.

Much more commonly, leaders feel animosity because of psychological, ideological, and value differences between themselves and their team members — differences perceived as a threat, no matter how exaggerated, irrational, or mistaken that perception turns out to be. In those cases, the animosity is less about what actually happened than about what the leader believes it to mean.

Each unpleasant exchange makes the next one easier to read as further proof of the other person’s flaws, until the leader is no longer responding to what the team member actually did but to an accumulated impression of who they are. Psychologists call this negative sentiment override, and once it takes hold, even neutral or well-intentioned behavior gets filtered through that lens.

Leaders will likely find some of the actions and behaviors of their team members annoying or irritating at times. But what commonly turns ordinary annoyance into animosity isn’t the behavior or its repetition, but the interpretation the leader assigns to it.

This means it can be addressed by changing how the leader interprets the behavior, independent of whether the team member changes anything at all. Leaders who want to overcome their animosity must learn to stop interpreting a team member’s actions as intentionally harmful and personally aimed at them.

t: A Letter to a Young Head of Department
q: Over the past few months I’ve had a series of increasingly depressing series of encounters with heads of English seeking on advice and guidance on how to contend with senior leaders who seem intent on making their lives as hard as possible. The following letter represents both my frustration and despair as well as a repository of all the pearls of wisdom I’ve tried to share.

By serious, I don’t mean solemn — solemnity is frequently the counterfeit of thought — I mean that you must preserve an allegiance to reality. Line managers may prefer a fog of intentions, but you need to develop a taste for facts.

Better to say, “Last time we met, we agreed that behaviour support would be arranged before the end of the week. That hasn’t happened, so I need to know whether the support is still coming or whether I’m expected to manage this without it.” Separate motive from effect.

People do struggle, and humane leadership requires more than pointing at standards and relying on shame. But standards must always remain visible, otherwise support becomes a place to hide rather than a route back to doing the job properly.

But, as you well know, a lesson isn’t good because it comes on a slide deck packaged with approved ‘dual coded’ logos but because it causes students to know something worth knowing or do something worth doing. Architecture that enables this is useful anything that prevents it is an obstacle course arranged in front of a fire exit.

We all wanted to be trusted but to be trustworthy you must be honest. Over committing — promising what you’d like to happen but which you know is unrealistic — is always worse than disappointing people at the outset.
Compromise can be a form of cowardice but, when intelligently chosen, it’s not surrender. Of course, your school is not a salon convened for the satisfaction of your ideals.

t: The Dashboard Delusion
q: And for as long as I can remember, CEOs have been looking for what I call the “God system.” This system would gather all the data about everything happening in the company, then present it in a way that lets the CEO make informed, near-perfect decisions. The new God system was a single view of all company analytics—revenue, pipeline, margin, hiring, churn, engagement.

Because in the future, AI will perform this exercise far better than any human ever could. If you are still chasing the fantasy of a God system for the CEO, you fundamentally view running the company as an information problem.
What it doesn’t tell you is: Are they running in the right direction? Are they making decisions aligned with your vision and strategy for the company?

Strategy is a hypothesis about how this company will win in a market that has not finished revealing itself. You can test pieces of it against evidence, but the bet itself is an act of judgment about conditions that have not occurred.

The answers are not in the data, because the answers are about the future that has to be chosen and created. Obsessive measuring of the past, and even the making of predictions based primarily on analysis of historical data, will not help you steer ahead.

t: One in Three Teachers Leave Within Five Years. Perhaps We're Asking the Wrong Question.
q: What if many early career teachers leave because they are never given the opportunity to become the teacher they hoped they would be?

Confidence rose after lessons that felt successful and meaningful, only to fall after difficult classroom experiences. Commitment strengthened when mentoring relationships were supportive and expectations were clear, but weakened when participants encountered inconsistent guidance or overwhelming pressure.

The problem emerges when evidence-informed practice quietly becomes evidence-enforced compliance. Instead of asking, What do these pupils need right now?, novice teachers may find themselves wondering, What does my observer want to see?

One participant moved from identifying herself as competent to feeling competent in nothing after experiencing overwhelming classroom pressures. Her sense of professional identity was shaken not because she lacked intelligence or commitment, but because the emotional realities of teaching overwhelmed an identity that was still under construction.
Perhaps they are not leaving because they dislike teaching. Perhaps they are leaving because they were never given enough time, trust or space to become teachers in the fullest sense of the word.

t: Designing a Predictive Talent Index Based on Your Best People
q: To evaluate and select talent, organizations naturally rely on personality assessments and psychological diagnostics to learn more about people. By digging deeper into the motivations, tendencies, and styles of prospective candidates and those up for promotion, leaders gain the data and confidence they need to make better choices.

As general predictors of how people will show up and behave once in a position, these assessments add a lot of value, which is one reason they are so popular. Because good leaders treat assessment results as another data point and not as a litmus test for selection, it is not uncommon for organizations to use multiple diagnostics at the same time.

But the best leaders and organizations have learned to take the fullest advantage of these assessments by using them more strategically. Leaders naturally want a true predictive tool to make their selections more accurate, so they turn to their best people to create one.

Finding a common pattern of that success can be a huge advantage in the selection process. The best leaders ask their top people to complete as many diagnostics and assessments as possible until a pattern correlated with success emerges.

For example, if an organization relies on the DISC assessment to test for features of personality, applying this tool to the best performers may reveal a pattern that can be used for prediction. If nearly all the organization’s top performers share a common set of personality results (in DISC, let’s say they are all High Ds and Cs), that pattern can now be used to find others with the same orientation.

Organizations can spend several years with a large set of assessment tools before they land on a pattern they have confidence in. But once they concoct that magic potion, it can significantly improve their selection process.
Organizations that do the work end up with more than a predictive tool. They create a mirror of what success in personality and style actually looks like in their culture.

t: Two Ways of Thinking, Two Explanation Challenges
q: The most recent posts about attention, context, and gist are now under the umbrella of Kahneman’s System 1 or “fast” thinking. In the post below, I’m using the recurring story of Olivia to set the stage for the next phase and a deeper dive into System 2 or “slow” thinking.
Her existing knowledge (context [ ]) helped her evaluate what was said. This created a substrate for memory to form, but this is only the beginning.
This is where we make a conscious effort to think something through. We apply reason and knowledge to construct an understanding of what we have experienced.

This deliberate reflection is System 2 thinking, and it can create action and long-term memories. This wasn’t necessarily a conscious decision, but a matter of competing priorities and a limited ability to process everything.

In fact, many researchers consider System 2 to be distinctly human. Having captured Olivia's attention and been deemed meaningful, the fiber advice became available for more deliberate thought, the kind of conscious reflection that System 2 makes possible.

It became part of cognitive science in the 1970s and gained widespread awareness from Kahneman’s book Thinking Fast and Slow. Why This Matters In the context of explanation, Systems 1 and 2 have real power because they show that explanations can fail for two very different reasons.
Further, thinking doesn’t happen in a pipeline, but in a progression. Nevertheless, there is compelling evidence that dual process theory captures important patterns in how we think.

t: The Trouble With Tech Abstinence
q: A major recent study [ ] from the National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER) examined one of the most popular [ ] school reforms of the moment: banning student cell phones. Using nationwide data from thousands of schools, researchers found that strict bans sharply reduced in-school phone use.
Student-reported feelings of well-being dipped, then improved. That pattern suggests something deeper than a simple gain or loss.

But it risks treating all screens as if they pose the same problems and offer the same educational value, or lack thereof. Schools were right to rediscover that attention matters and that not every instructional problem calls for a screen-based solution.

As instructional coach Zach Groshell recently argued [ ], the Chromebook often became less a learning tool than a classroom babysitter—a way to occupy students rather than teach them. That said, substituting activity for learning didn’t start with computers.

Schools have spent decades pretending this can be done effectively; AI does it effortlessly. I have seen AI systems give students detailed, actionable feedback on their writing—sometimes identifying weaknesses and patterns that I missed, even as a former teacher and professional writer.
It is nearly effortless on the student’s part and nearly impossible for educators to catch. AI creates a temptation for not only students but also schools.

Less prepared or motivated students may use it as a substitute for thinking, outsourcing judgment to systems they lack the knowledge to evaluate critically. In this way, AI may amplify the very inequalities it is uniquely well suited to solve.

t: The Science of Reading in High School: Engaging Rhetorical Exemplars in the ELA Classroom
q: In contemporary public discourse, it’s clear that many people have not been taught how to argue effectively. Name-calling, groundless accusations, guilt by association, and other logical fallacies are sprinkled throughout the news, social media, and conversations.

Each semester, I thought of this unit as my small attempt to address this broader problem by at least introducing the students in my class to a better way. The core of the unit was the pairing of two seminal rhetorical texts: “Letter to Viceroy, Lord Irwin” by Mohandas Gandhi [ ] and “Letter from a Birmingham Jail” by Dr.

I would begin the unit with Gandhi’s letter, since it preceded King and served as an inspiration for his nonviolent direct action during the Civil Rights Movement. After guiding my students through a close reading of the text and developing a summary paragraph, I would direct their attention to the rhetorical devices for a second look at the text using a jigsaw activity.

Following this, I would call on members from each group to share an example of each rhetorical device, and I would restate and clarify the way each example demonstrated an effective use of rhetoric. Lastly, after our whole class discussion, students would complete a SOAPSTone analysis chart and paragraph to synthesize their thinking about Gandhi’s message and his use of rhetoric.

First, given the length of the letter, I would strategically scaffold the reading of the text. To start, I would set our expectations and direct students to look for and annotate certain elements in King’s prose.

Finally, I would have students write a gist or summary statement for the first eleven paragraphs. This prepares students to engage in a similar routine that they will complete in groups as we jigsawed the remaining paragraphs of the letter.

Lastly, one element of their assessment over this unit was a written comparison of the use of rhetoric in the two texts. This assignment helps students demonstrate their analysis and argumentation skills, their ability to cite and interpret text evidence, and practice synthesizing information from two separate sources.

t: Summer Refinement Series, Post 4: Refining Knowledge Organizers to Build Automaticity
q: Last year was my first year implementing knowledge organizers. They are definitely one of the most important instructional tools I use.

Previously, I was primarily concerned with whether I had included what students should know. Instead of trying to add every relevant term or example, I now ask this question to determine what makes it on the page: What knowledge do students need to be able to retrieve so fluently that it is automatic?

When foundational knowledge and vocabulary has been securely stored in long-term memory and can be retrieved effortlessly, students no longer have to devote valuable working memory resources to recalling and using that information. Instead, those resources become available for more expert-level knowledge building and thinking.
Endless definitions, examples, and facts found their way onto the page because I believed everything was essential. Looking back, I was designing more for coverage rather than for automaticity.

In other words, my knowledge organizers will prioritize only the information students need to know, not the information that’s simply nice to know. A Concrete Example: Micro-Entrepreneurs in Africa The knowledge organizer for our Micro-Entrepreneurs: Women’s Role in the Development of Africa case study shows this refinement concretely.

All of these appear repeatedly throughout the case study and become the domain-specific language and knowledge-base students will need to use to learn and understand increasingly complex ideas. If students cannot retrieve these ideas and their definitions automatically, they will struggle to master their meaning.

Instead of adding every country discussed in the case study, I purposefully selected Mali, Uganda, and Botswana because each can serve as a cognitive hook in long-term memory for a broader, more complicated concept. Mali is associated with multifunctional platforms and quality of life.

t: Nonexperts Use the Wrong Criteria to Make Selections of Quality
q: Many of an organization’s worst decisions aren’t made by incompetent people. They are made by smart, confident people who are nonexperts in the domain where they have decision-making authority.

They don’t decide wrongly because they ignore important criteria but because they give too much weight to superficial attributes, such as brand, social proof, and likeability, and too little weight to the performance criteria most important to true experts. Research reveals that nonexperts also prioritize immediate outcomes, such as short-term comfort and speed of implementation, over long-term effectiveness, established track record, and strategic fit.

Instead of asking, “Is this program or vendor good?” they ask, “Does this feel right to me?” They know that feeling right is much easier to defend in a meeting than being right. This is one reason so many low-quality programs, experts, and experiences are brought into organizations and become deeply entrenched over years.

For instance, when marketing experts make artistic decisions, or when human resources experts decide between artificial intelligence tools, they depend too heavily on what others are doing rather than doing the work to discern quality and performance. Busy leaders make the same poor decisions when they stray from their core expertise.

Of course, this leads to poor choices across any domain where they lack true expertise. Nonexperts are drawn to cues that are easy to interpret, like brand familiarity, visual polish, or social media reviews.

So, brand familiarity, visual polish, and social media reviews crowd out more objective measures of quality when they make decisions regarding which programs, people, and tools to bring into the organization. Over time, these weak choices can have a tremendously negative impact on the overall quality of the organization.

The tragedy is that it feels indistinguishable from good judgment to the person exercising it. A confident choice predicated on superficial criteria carries all the emotional weight of a well-reasoned one, which is precisely what makes it so dangerous.

t: Is Good Practice Too Babyish for Big Kids? Or Is That Just a Teacher Misconception?
q: If you’re reading this blog, you’re probably already familiar with the evidence underpinning cognitive load theory, explicit instruction, knowledge-rich curriculum and behaviour routines. t: Introducing the EEF Guide to Inclusive Teaching
q: Read more ( I The two-part model ( The guide introduces a practical two-part framework: * Universal approaches – evidence-informed classroom practices that benefit every pupil and are particularly important for pupils with additional needs. * Adaptations and additional support – classroom adaptations, small-group teaching, one-to-one support and targeted interventions used where needed to enable pupils to access high-quality teaching.

Strengthening and sustaining these approaches is likely to benefit all pupils and can reduce, though not remove, the need for additional support. Drawing on the best available evidence, the guide highlights five areas of universal practice: * Explicit instruction: clear, well-sequenced teaching that supports all pupils to access new learning.

* Positive relationships: predictable, supportive interactions that help pupils feel safe and ready to learn. * Calm classroom environments: routines and settings that reduce unnecessary barriers to participation.

But it is important to recognise that adaptations and additional support can be effective or ineffective, and that ineffective support or adaptation can hinder learning. For example, oversimplifying tasks in ways that reduce pupils' thinking can limit learning.

Explore effective and ineffective adaptations ( I Inclusive teaching myth-busting ( We address some of the most common misconceptions about inclusive teaching: * Inclusive teaching is all about what schools do differently for pupils with additional needs. * The more adaptations teachers make, the more pupils will learn.

* Teachers need specialist expertise before they can effectively support pupils with additional needs. By addressing these misconceptions directly, the guide encourages schools to focus on evidence-informed approaches that strengthen teaching for all pupils while providing effective additional support where needed.

t: Exploring Adaptive Teaching
q: Over recent years, adaptive teaching has become one of the most frequently used phrases in education. It appears in policy documents, professional development programmes, Ofsted discussions and research literature.

Instead, adaptive teaching describes what highly effective teachers have always done: gathering evidence about learning and using that information to make precise adjustments to instruction so that all pupils can successfully access ambitious curriculum content. The Education Endowment Foundation’s new Guide to Inclusive Teaching [ ] reinforces this understanding.

Responsiveness to Evidence of Learning Teachers actively seek information about what pupils know, understand and can do through questioning, assessment, feedback and observation. They then use this evidence to inform instructional decisions.

High-quality adaptive teaching therefore sits at the intersection of both How Do Our Teaching PiPs Support Adaptive and Inclusive Teaching? The Durrington Teaching Principles in Practice (TPiPs) provide the mechanism through which adaptive and inclusive teaching happens in classrooms every day.
Teachers gain reliable information about readiness for new learning. This reflects the EEF’s emphasis on establishing strong universal classroom routines that support participation for all pupils.

Instruction responds to specific learning needs rather than broad assumptions. This reflects the EEF’s argument that effective adaptations should be informed by ongoing assessment and linked directly to learning needs.

Gathering Responses Mini whiteboards, hinge questions and other response systems provide real-time data. Teachers can then decide whether to: Re-teach a concept Provide another example Increase challenge Add a scaffold Offer further guided practice This exemplifies the EEF’s recommendation that adaptations should often involve increasing the intensity of high-quality teaching rather than changing its fundamental nature.

t: Chess, Blind Rage, and Education
q: Unable to stand the frustration of losing another game of chess, I slammed shut my laptop and summoned all of my self-control to keep from punching my desk. I wish I could say this was an isolated incident, but I have been in this situation dozens of times in my life.

Thinking, “This lesson is not that difficult, so there is no reason students should be confused,” creates emotional distance between the teacher and the learning—or lack of learning—happening in the classroom. If a lesson is not that difficult, then it must be the student’s fault for not understanding.

Hold that format in your mind — three hours, standing, on the most explosive question in American life — the next time someone with a mute button and a sixty-second shot clock tells you you’re watching a “debate.” The tradition held long enough to pass the hardest test the twentieth century gave it.

It is the precise instant the American system failed — force substituted for rebuttal — and admirers across the South mailed Brooks replacement canes [ ] to congratulate him. Five years later came the war, and roughly 750,000 dead [ ] settled a question that Congress had first refused to debate and then proved unable to.

And at this moment, that question is being settled the way the gag-rule Congress settled slavery: by not arguing it. The real decisions are made by default — by release schedules, capital expenditure, and competitive pressure — while public argument gets waved off from one side as doomer hysteria and from the other as Luddite cope.

Summer is the season to notice what is right with it: thousands of kids choosing, on their own vacation, to think harder than school requires, about the most consequential questions in the country, under an obligation to understand the people they disagree with. t: Leading Team Members Who Start Out Strong But Fizzle Out Over Time
q: Team members who start out strong, demonstrate their skills through results, and appear to settle comfortably into the culture are a big win for leaders. But over time, these capable people sometimes lose their momentum, begin to underperform, and seem very different from the persona they projected early on.

Leading team members who begin powerfully but fizzle out over time is both highly disappointing and a unique challenge for leaders. There are many reasons a team member’s performance can drop off a cliff after a couple of years of strong results — some preventable, others coachable, and a few that may well be unchangeable.
The first task of the leader is to generate a theory as to why. Exploring this reality, no matter how uncomfortable it might be for both parties, is the place to start formulating an explanation.

Among the most common explanations for this performance arc is a mismatch between the role and the person’s evolving ambitions. People grow, and what once excited and challenged the team member may no longer hold the same appeal.

When the role remains static even as the person develops new interests, stronger skills, or broader aspirations, disengagement becomes almost inevitable. Leaders who surface this possibility early often discover that a modest adjustment in responsibilities, scope, or opportunity is all that is needed to reignite the energy and output that once defined the team member’s contribution.

A second and more difficult explanation involves the team member’s relationship with the organization itself. Sometimes what fizzles is not the person’s competence but their confidence in leadership, their belief in the mission, or their trust in the culture they once embraced.

It is rarely announced and easily mistaken for laziness or indifference. Sometimes the disengagement can be rectified by exploring why they have come to believe what they do and advocating for a different frame or interpretation of the events and incidents that created their distrust.

t: ISTE Endorses Speech & Debate
q: As of June 28 [ ], it stands for the International Society for Transforming Education. CEO Richard Culatta’s explanation was blunt: we can’t keep doing assessment the way we used to [ ], can’t keep teaching the way we used to, and a name about the tool no longer describes the work.

Debate is one of the last places in a teenager’s life where the “problematic not to use your own mind” muscle gets loaded to failure on purpose. We have endless conversations about teaching students to use AI well.

They are self-directed learners by necessity, which is precisely the disposition that lets a student treat an AI tutor as an accelerant instead of a crutch. The framework wants students who can clarify a challenge, generate options, and evaluate solutions.

A debater who has spent a season getting punished in-round for reading a weak card does not take a confident-sounding AI summary at face value. They’ve been burned by fluent, authoritative text before — and that scar tissue is the whole point.

The debater takes 40-90 minutes of clash, decides which two arguments actually matter, collapses everything else, and re-pitches the entire round to the specific person holding the ballot — in five minutes. That is synthesis under pressure, which is the only kind of synthesis the real world ever actually asks for.
You cannot tell when an AI’s argument is weak unless you can build a strong one. You cannot catch a dishonest synthesis unless you’ve sweated through honest ones.

t: How Senior Leaders Can Lead Learning in Schools
q: The most important question for a senior leader is not, 'What did I see?' but, 'Where is the system least aligned?'
A compliance culture asks whether learning walks have happened, whether data has been entered and whether meetings have taken place. An improvement culture asks what those activities changed.

Cold calling is not effective because it is visible during an observation. It is effective when it increases thinking, makes participation more equitable and helps the teacher gather information about understanding.

If Year 10 outcomes in a subject are weaker than expected, leaders should resist jumping straight to more monitoring or more intervention. They might instead ask whether pupils are failing to remember core knowledge.
The loop is not complete when evidence has been collected. It is complete when teaching changes and pupils know, remember or can do more.

t: Faded Scaffolding: Keeping Challenge High While Building Independence
q: A scaffold is successful when it becomes less necessary. The danger is not the scaffold itself, but the permanent scaffold: the support that stays so long pupils learn to complete the prompt rather than think, write, read or solve independently.
If the task is too easy, the scaffold is unnecessary. If the task has been simplified until pupils no longer meet the core demand, support has slipped into low expectations.

Fading is not a sudden jump from full support to no support. It is a series of professional decisions based on evidence of readiness. The question is not, Have I used a scaffold? but, What information tells me that this scaffold can now be reduced, narrowed or removed?

One mutation is the permanent crutch, where the support stays forever and pupils learn the routine rather than the strategy. Another is the worksheet mutation, where scaffolding becomes extra paper rather than better modelling, questioning or checking.
Faded scaffolding is not about doing less for pupils. It is about using the right support at the right time, then reducing it when evidence shows they are ready.

t: Behind Every Great School
q: Summer is a time for reflection for me, and lately the need for great leadership in schools has been at the top of my mind. So this post is for the leaders who made me, and every teacher they’ve worked with, a better teacher.

She had a clear vision, clear expectations for what good teaching looked like, clear standards for what kids should be doing and learning. But, and this is the part so many leaders miss, she backed those expectations with the time, support and tools to meet them.
She had promised to balance classrooms if I stayed in 4th instead of moving down to 3rd. But the new hire didn’t have gifted-and-talented certification.

In observations, she’d sit in the back of the classroom with an absolutely unreadable face, and I’d spend the whole lesson spiraling. But that was the thing: she actually watched, and she actually paid attention.

I avoid it like the plague, and if I’m honest, that single trait alone probably cancels out any other quality I have that might make me good in the role. But in her ever-reassuring way, she insisted I had the right skill set and spent the following two years encouraging me to move beyond the classroom.

Declining enrollment hit this school hard, and once again I had to leave a school and community I loved, despite my principal’s best attempts to advocate to keep me. Year 20: All of the Above Before landing here, I feared education had turned into something that wasn’t sustainable, and that the leaders of the past were just that.

They made sure every child could say out loud, “I feel safe and seen here,” and mean it, not just say it because it was expected. And these women, who I am so lucky to have had in my life, were the great ones.

t: AI: Helping Students Join the Conversation
q: At the recent Oracy Conference here in my college at Cambridge, Hughes Hall, I found myself talking with Kate Paradine, CEO of Voice 21, about the new report, chaired by Estelle Morris, on why white working-class children are being left behind in education. Mothers in Grimsby interviewed by the BBC were saying that what mattered to them was not “education”, but work.

In my college I meet people working in medicine, law, architecture, engineering, business and public policy, most of them deeply engaged with hospitals, industry, government and communities. If even Cambridge, supposedly the peak of academia, is full of people connecting knowledge with practice, why does school still feel to so many families as if it is a detour from reality?

Why should this be reserved for adults already inside elite professional worlds? Imagine a mathematics lesson in which students run a market stall — pricing stock, working out wastage, and deciding whether to extend credit to a regular customer, while a rival stallholder undercuts them and the council warden threatens a fine.

The idea is to augment the existing knowledge-focused curriculum — perhaps accelerated with AI but with teachers guiding and framing throughout — and to show how that knowledge can be applied to understand real world situations and solve real world problems. Most of what human beings learn, we do not learn from books or formal lessons.

My own work on dialogic education has been inspired partly by Michael Oakeshott, who taught history for many years at Gonville and Caius College, Cambridge, and described education as joining “the conversation of mankind”. But we need to widen Oakeshott’s image beyond history, philosophy and classics.
We inherit long conversations: mathematics, science, history, literature, technology, craft, politics, religion and work. They are living traditions of argument, evidence, judgement and practice.
The third loop is deferred indefinitely: learn this now, you may need it later. AI-supported, multi-voiced cases could bring all three loops together.
